concepts.def: Wire with current in field feels a force.
Moving wire near magnet makes voltage.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Put a wire carrying current inside a magnetic field. The wire feels a force.

This is the motor effect.

If we coil the wire and let it spin, we have an electric motor.

Motors are in fans, drills, washing machines, electric cars, drones - everywhere!

A generator does the opposite. Move a wire through a magnetic field - and electricity is created!

This is called electromagnetic induction.

Power stations use this: steam spins a magnet, magnet spins past coils, electricity flows out. Coal, gas, nuclear, wind and hydro stations all do this same final step.

MRI scanners: a huge electromagnet maps the body without X-rays.

Maglev trains: float and zoom above a track on repelling electromagnets.

Hard drives: store data as tiny magnetic patches.

Phones: contain mini magnets in vibration motors and speakers.

mcqs.q: If an object is moving at constant velocity in a straight line, what is the net force on it?
options: Zero — by Newton's first law, constant velocity requires zero net force.
Velocity is always conserved in any collision.
The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
There must be a forward force on the object to keep it moving.

mcqs.q: In a collision between two objects, what quantity is always conserved (in a closed system)?
options: The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
Total momentum is always conserved; kinetic energy is only conserved in elastic collisions.
Velocity is always conserved in any collision.
Kinetic energy is always conserved in collisions because energy is conserved.

mcqs.q: In which direction does an electric field point near a positive charge?
options: Radially outwards — the field is defined by the force on a positive test charge, which is repelled.
Radially inwards because positive attracts negative.
There is no field around a positive charge unless another charge is present.
The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
